source: Bouwmeester et al. (2017) Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene, and Nowak (2012)
finding: Large multi-lab replication of the claim that fast intuitive responding raises cooperation. Under the main intent-to-treat test the effect was zero.
numbers: 3,596 students, 21 labs, 12 countries. Time pressure minus delay: -0.37 points (95% CI -2.60 to 1.86). Original: 8.6 points (49.4% vs 40.8%). Lab heterogeneity I2=2.72%.
quote: the RRR does not provide evidence for an effect of speeded versus delayed responses on cooperation.
limits: One-shot public goods game; 10-second cutoff is arbitrary; labs individually underpowered.
agent_relevance: A famous 'fast = X, slow = Y' result failed at scale. Do not build agent rules on a speed-to-behaviour link without a pooled test.

source: Bouwmeester et al. (2017) Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene, and Nowak (2012)
finding: Why the original looked positive: only compliant participants showed a gap, and compliance was very uneven, so the gap is likely selection bias.
numbers: Compliant only: gap 10.37 points (original 15.31). Compliance: 34.1% in time pressure vs 92.5% in forced delay. Excluding prior-experience players: -2.19; excluding failed comprehension: -0.64.
limits: Compliant-only analysis breaks random assignment.
agent_relevance: Dropping 'non-compliant' runs from a speed or budget manipulation can create a false effect. Analyse all runs as assigned (intent to treat).

source: Rehren (2024) Meta-analysis: cognitive load, ego depletion, induction, time restriction and moral judgments on sacrificial dilemmas
finding: Meta-analysis of manipulations meant to cut deliberation (Greene's dual-process model of moral judgment). Pooled effect on utilitarian choice is near zero and not significant.
numbers: 44 articles, 68 studies, N=14,003. Pooled Hedges g=0.06 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.12, p=.057). Personal dilemmas g=0.03; high-conflict personal g=0.05. Process-dissociation subset (12 studies, N=2,577) g=0.11 (CI -0.01 to 0.23).
limits: Substantial heterogeneity (Q(108)=433.17). Mood manipulations excluded.
agent_relevance: Cutting a human's deliberation barely changes the answer here. Weak support that 'more thinking' systematically reroutes judgment.

source: Rehren (2024) Meta-analysis: cognitive load, ego depletion, induction, time restriction and moral judgments on sacrificial dilemmas
finding: Publication bias is visible. Corrected estimates fall to zero or below. Effects are larger in student and European samples.
numbers: Egger p=.001. Trim-and-fill (17 imputed studies) g=-0.02 (CI -0.09 to 0.05). PET-PEESE g=-0.11 (p=.007, likely over-corrects). European samples g=0.15 (p=.002); student samples g=0.15 (p=.014); grey literature g=-0.05.
limits: Author says PET-PEESE over-corrects.
agent_relevance: Treat published small effects of 'load' manipulations as inflated. Our own tests should include unpublished null runs.

source: Untested Assumptions and Tenuous Evidence: A Critique of the Dual-Process Account of Moral Judgment (2025)
finding: Review of the moral dual-process claim. Reports that a 2016 study with over 1,400 people found neither cognitive load nor time pressure changed 'do something' choices (Tinghog et al. 2016).
numbers: Tinghog et al. 2016: >1,400 participants, no effect of load or time pressure. Gawronski & Beer reanalysis: load and time pressure increased 'do something' choices, the opposite of the model's prediction.
limits: Secondary report of other studies; no new data. Authors of the review include a rival-theory developer.
agent_relevance: Direction of the effect of reduced deliberation is itself unstable. A 'fast = emotional' rule can predict the wrong sign.

source: Untested Assumptions and Tenuous Evidence: A Critique of the Dual-Process Account of Moral Judgment (2025)
finding: Speed does not tell you which kind of process produced an answer. In the two-response paradigm, fast first answers were often already the 'slow' kind.
numbers: Bago & De Neys (2019): about 74% of response pairs were utilitarian-utilitarian, about 11% deontological then utilitarian, about 10% deontological-deontological. UU was 87.5% of all second utilitarian responses.
limits: Reported secondhand in the critique; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Fast output can be correct without a slow stage. Do not assume the slow check is what fixes an answer; log first and final answers separately.

source: Untested Assumptions and Tenuous Evidence: A Critique of the Dual-Process Account of Moral Judgment (2025)
finding: Item and response-bias problems: the classic dilemma set is not a clean contrast, and real behavior differs from hypothetical choices.
numbers: Kahane & Shackel: philosophers judged only 45% (impersonal) and 48% (personal) items to be real utilitarian-vs-deontological conflicts. McGuire 2009: dropping items where under 5% gave 'inappropriate' answers removed the effect. Bostyn et al. 2018: deontological choice 34% hypothetical vs 16% real (5 mice vs 1).
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Check that a test set actually separates the two answer types before reading results as evidence about processes.

source: Untested Assumptions and Tenuous Evidence: A Critique of the Dual-Process Account of Moral Judgment (2025)
finding: Rival accounts that need no two systems: parallel comparison (Gurcay & Baron) and a response-bias account. Baron & Gurcay meta-analysis found no convincing evidence of a fast response being overridden.
numbers: Review says the dual-process moral model is hard to falsify ('very little convincing evidence'). Tremoliere & Bonnefon: load effect at a 1:5 kill ratio but none at 1:500.
limits: Critique, not neutral.
agent_relevance: Competing single-process accounts predict the same speed effects. An agent design should not depend on the two-system story to work.

source: Mega & Volz (2014) Thinking about thinking: implications of the introspective error for default-interventionist type models of dual processes
finding: Editorial that proposes a 'default-disruptive' view: putting intuition into words can damage it rather than correct it. Cites verbal overshadowing and reasons-analysis studies.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990 (describing a robber hurt later face identification) and Wilson & Schooler 1991 (analysing reasons worsened course choices).
limits: Editorial; the authors call it a preliminary approximation; limited to non-verbalizable experience.
agent_relevance: Rival to the default-interventionist model; predicts that forced written reasoning can hurt on perceptual or pattern tasks. Tested in LLMs by Liu et al. 2025 (b21-b23).

source: Otero et al. (2024) Sex differences in cognitive reflection: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of cognitive reflection tests (CRT, the bat-and-ball type). A small male advantage on numerical tests, almost none on verbal ones.
numbers: 77 documents. Numerical: 112 effect sizes, N=66,109, d=0.39, corrected delta=0.47 (CI 0.44 to 0.50). Verbal: 25 effect sizes, N=9,916, delta=0.13 (CI 0.06 to 0.19). Artifacts explain about 37% of numerical variance.
limits: Correlational; gap may be numeracy or math anxiety, not reflection; time-limited tests excluded.
agent_relevance: The CRT mixes reflection with numeracy. Using it as the 'System 2' gauge for an LLM over-reads arithmetic skill.

source: Otero et al. (2021) Criterion validity of cognitive reflection for predicting job performance and training proficiency: a meta-analysis
finding: Cognitive reflection predicts work outcomes moderately, but adds little beyond general intelligence.
numbers: Job performance: 7 coefficients, N=1,508, r=.28, true validity rho=.36 (CI .26 to .46). Training: 15 coefficients, N=3,705, rho=.37. Multiple R over intelligence: .440 to .465 (job), .620 to .622 (training).
limits: Few primary studies; no supervisor ratings; meta-analytic matrix regression.
agent_relevance: The reflective disposition is real but overlaps with ability. Scaffold gains should be compared against a stronger base model, not just a bare one.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2022) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: Older GPT-3 models fell for the CRT trap more often than people. ChatGPT and GPT-4 largely did not.
numbers: Trap answers on CRT: 80% for GPT-3-davinci-003 vs 55% for humans; 15% ChatGPT-3.5; 0% ChatGPT-4. Correct: 5% davinci-003, 59% ChatGPT-3.5, 96% ChatGPT-4 vs 38% humans. Human baseline from original study (n=3,428) was 41% correct.
limits: Items may be in training data; some items re-worded; v1 of the preprint.
agent_relevance: Trap-susceptibility is a property of the model tier, not a fixed trait. Re-measure for each model we use.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2022) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: Forcing step-by-step text acts like a System 2 switch for weaker models. Blocking it hurts weaker models little and GPT-4 only slightly.
numbers: davinci-003 told to reason step by step: correct 5% to 28%, trap answers 80% to 29%. Blocking chain-of-thought: ChatGPT-3.5 correct change not significant (-4%); ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, trap answers 0% to 10%. ChatGPT-4 solved 24% of CRT without chain-of-thought in Study 1.
limits: Small item set; chi-square tests on item counts.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous reasoning text marks slow mode in LLMs; a strong model can answer correctly without it, so the text is not required for correctness.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2022) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: Few-shot examples teach the 'intuition': accuracy jumped with a handful of training examples. Semantic illusions show the same pattern.
numbers: CRT-like tasks: accuracy 2% to 92% after two examples; 12% to 92% after seven; another task 0% to about 78% after 30 examples. Semantic illusions: trap answers 72% for davinci-003; correct 18% to 74% (ChatGPT-3.5) and 88% (ChatGPT-4); with CoT, davinci correct 18% to 54%.
limits: Examples may have been close to test items.
agent_relevance: Examples in the prompt change 'intuition' strongly; a scaffold step with examples may beat a reflection step on trap tasks.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 answered all three CRT items with the intuitive wrong answer, and still gave the wrong answer when the item was lightly rewritten.
numbers: All 3 CRT items answered intuitively wrong. Told 'the bat costs $1.00 more than the bat' (altered item), it still said the ball costs $0.10.
limits: Earliest model; one prompt wording per item.
agent_relevance: Pass or fail on a memorised CRT item says little about reasoning. Use altered items.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and logic
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own tests: written reasoning (CoT, the closest LLM analogue of System 2) helps mostly on math, symbolic and logic tasks, and little elsewhere.
numbers: Mean CoT gains: symbolic reasoning +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9 points. Other categories: 56.8 with CoT vs 56.1 without. On MMLU, up to 95% of the CoT gain comes from questions containing an equals sign.
limits: Averages over published papers; selection of papers may bias.
agent_relevance: Gate deliberate reasoning by task type. Spending slow steps on non-symbolic questions is wasted.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and logic
finding: Most of the CoT gain is in carrying out symbolic steps, and a solver tool beats CoT there.
numbers: Paper reports the CoT gain on symbolic tasks comes mostly from executing steps, and a symbolic solver outperformed CoT on planning-style tasks.
limits: Specific tasks; tool use not tested everywhere.
agent_relevance: Prefer code or a solver for the slow step over more text where the task is formal.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend huge compute on trivial questions. The first solution is usually already right.
numbers: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 'what is 2 plus 3?'. In more than 92% of cases on tested sets the first solution round was already correct.
limits: Mostly math sets (ASDIV, MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA, AIME); QwQ-32B and R1 class models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for an adaptive switch: the agent needs a cheap check for 'easy' so it does not run the full slow path.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Training a model on its own filtered slow-method outputs can move slow-method accuracy into a fast direct answer on some tasks, not all.
numbers: Last-letter concatenation: zero-shot 30.0%, System 2 (2-step RaR) 39.5% at 106.6 tokens, distilled 98.0% at 25.5 tokens. Coin flip: 56.1% base; 1-step RaR 77.2%; distilled 2-step RaR 75.69%. S2A bias task: zero-shot 51.6%, S2A 76.0%, distilled 81.3% (56 tokens vs 147).
limits: Needs training; our agent is scaffold-only. Chain-of-thought math tasks did not distill well per the paper.
agent_relevance: Shows slow methods are worth keeping only when the answer is checkable; no training for us.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: Regenerating the context to remove irrelevant or opinionated text before answering raises factuality and accuracy with distractors.
numbers: Factuality with a distractor opinion 62.8% to 80.3% (LLaMA-2-70B-chat); objectivity of long-form up 57.4%; math with irrelevant sentences 51.7% to 61.3%.
limits: Costs an extra generation pass; evaluated on LLaMA-2-70B-chat.
agent_relevance: A concrete 'deliberate cleaning step' that works and matches our restating operator.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Tests the default-disruptive idea: tasks where verbal thinking hurts people also see CoT hurt models in three of six tasks.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar): GPT-4o 94.00% direct vs 57.70% for o1-preview on a subset, drop up to 36.3 points. Full set: GPT-4o 87.5% to 64.4% (-23.1), Claude 3 Opus 70.7 to 62.7 (-8.0), Gemini 1.5 Pro -6.05; Claude 3.5 Sonnet +1.8 (not significant).
limits: Six tasks only; models and humans differ on memory and priors; some tasks showed no harm.
agent_relevance: Slow reasoning is not a free upgrade. Pattern and perception tasks may do worse with written reasoning.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Face recognition with similar distractors and learning labels with exceptions also fell with CoT.
numbers: Face recognition: GPT-4o 64.0% to 51.2% (-12.8), Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6 (-14.4), Gemini 1.5 Pro -11.4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8. Exceptions task: GPT-4o needed 2.9 rounds direct vs 12.5 with CoT (+331% relative).
limits: Task adapted from a human study.
agent_relevance: Add a task-type screen: perceptual or exception-heavy tasks get the fast path with a check, not default CoT.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Where humans lack knowledge that models have, CoT helps the model even though thinking hurts people.
numbers: Logical-inconsistency (NLI), spatial intuition and working-memory tasks showed mixed or neutral CoT effects. Authors explain: models have logic priors and long context.
limits: Explanations are post hoc.
agent_relevance: The human analogy predicts risk but not outcome. Measure per task.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Longer reasoning can lower accuracy. Claude Opus 4 and DeepSeek R1 drop on simple counting with distractors as reasoning grows.
numbers: Claude Opus 4: accuracy from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning lengthens. DeepSeek R1 (natural overthinking): 70% to 30% with five distractors. o3 more stable. Five failure modes named incl. spurious correlations and loss of focus on deduction.
limits: Constructed tasks; effect depends on model family.
agent_relevance: Cap reasoning length and compare short vs long runs for each task class.

source: Su et al. (2025) Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking by learning with randomized reasoning traces
finding: A single model trained with randomly dropped reasoning traces can run in fast, slow or auto mode on maze and math tasks.
numbers: Slow: 97.6% optimal on 30x30 mazes vs Searchformer 93.3%, 45.5% fewer steps. Fast: 80% vs solution-only 30%. Auto: 96.6% optimal with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Synthetic maze tasks; trained models, not a prompting scaffold. Only the abstract was read closely.
agent_relevance: Supports a switch between fast and slow modes; the gain comes with training, so our scaffold must rely on a program-side gate.

source: Agent synthesis of b01-b25 (no new source)
finding: Pattern across the evidence: the fast/slow distinction is useful as a design heuristic for compute allocation, but the human time-pressure and load evidence is weak (b01-b08), so the theory is not a safe basis for rules.
numbers: Human side: replication null (N=3,596), meta-analysis g=0.06 (N=14,003). LLM side: CoT +14.2 on symbolic, +0.7 elsewhere; harm up to -36.3 on some tasks.
limits: Synthesis written by the agent; not a source.
agent_relevance: Use dual-process language only as 'cheap path first, expensive path when a code-side check says so'.
